description: Test your knowledge of PA H5 | Hemolytic Anemias with key concepts on classification, mechanisms, and laboratory findings.

cards.text: Define haemolysis. How does it differ from haemolytic anaemia?
cards.answer: Haemolysis is premature RBC destruction before 120 days (physiological or pathological). Haemolytic anaemia occurs when destruction exceeds the bone marrow's compensatory capacity, resulting in falling haemoglobin and clinical symptoms.

tip.tip: Haemolysis = RBC death; Anaemia = failure to replace them fast enough

cards.text: What is the bone marrow's compensatory reserve in response to haemolysis? What happens if it fails?
cards.answer: The marrow can increase erythropoiesis 6–8 fold. If destruction outpaces this maximal output, clinical anaemia supervenes with fatigue, pallor, and dyspnoea.

tip.tip: 6–8× reserve = starting point; intercurrent infections or folate deficiency can tip the balance

cards.text: Distinguish compensated from decompensated haemolytic states.
cards.answer: Compensated: RBC lifespan shortened (30–60 days) but marrow output maintains normal Hb; patient mild jaundice/splenomegaly but not anaemic (can persist years). Decompensated: destruction exceeds marrow compensation; Hb falls, clinical anaemia develops.

tip.tip: Compensated = fight on; decompensated = losing battle

cards.text: Which site accounts for 80–85% of all haemolysis? Describe the mechanism.
cards.answer: Extravascular haemolysis in the mononuclear phagocyte system (spleen, liver, bone marrow). Macrophages recognise altered RBCs (membrane protein defects, abnormal shape, surface IgG/C3b) and engulf them intact. Haemoglobin is catabolised inside the macrophage.

tip.tip: Extravascular = macrophages eat the cell; haemoglobin broken down inside

cards.text: Name three key lab findings in extravascular haemolysis.
cards.answer: ↑ Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin → jaundice; ↑ urine urobilinogen; normal plasma haemoglobin; **absent** haemoglobinuria; splenomegaly.

tip.tip: Think 'intact cell → bilirubin traffic'; no free Hb in plasma = no haemoglobinuria

cards.text: How does intravascular haemolysis differ mechanistically from extravascular? Give two examples.
cards.answer: RBC membrane ruptures directly within blood vessels (not engulfed by macrophages). Free haemoglobin is released into plasma. Examples: PNH (complement-mediated lysis), G6PD crisis, prosthetic heart valve (mechanical MAHA), DIC/TTP (microangiopathic).

tip.tip: Intravascular = cells burst *in situ*; free Hb floods the plasma

cards.text: Name three key lab findings unique to intravascular haemolysis.
cards.answer: ↑ Plasma free haemoglobin (markedly); ↓ serum haptoglobin (saturated binding free Hb); **haemoglobinuria** (red/brown urine); chronic form → urinary haemosiderin (Prussian blue-positive tubular casts).

tip.tip: Free Hb → binds haptoglobin → Hb passes glomerulus → pee turns rust-coloured

cards.text: Distinguish hereditary from acquired haemolytic anaemias by definition and typical presentation.
cards.answer: Hereditary: intrinsic RBC defects (membrane, enzyme, haemoglobin), almost always intracorpuscular, present in childhood/early adulthood, lifelong, positive family history. Acquired: external factors (antibodies, infections, drugs), may be intracorpuscular or extracorpuscular, any age, usually no family history.

tip.tip: Hereditary = the cell's fault; Acquired = the world's fault
